Smooth Muscle Physiology

Lecture Companion · Ruchi Patel, PhD · Original course figures embedded

Learning objectivesStructureCa²⁺ couplingRegulationVascular controlComparison

The big picture and learning objectives

Contraction follows a single central chain: Ca²⁺ → calmodulin → MLCK → phosphorylated myosin. But smooth muscle can initiate or modify that chain through electrical, chemical, hormonal, mechanical and autonomic inputs.

  1. Structure, function, sites, and single-unit versus multi-unit muscle
  2. Excitation–contraction coupling, calcium, calmodulin, MLCK, MLCP versus skeletal muscle
  3. Nervous, hormonal and local chemical regulation
  4. Vascular dilator and constrictor pathways
Course content · section 1

The structural design of smooth muscle

Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped, nonstriated cells with a single central nucleus. They contain actin, myosin and tropomyosin, but no troponin. Actin attaches to dense bodies and membrane-associated anchoring structures. Those structures transmit force without an orderly sarcomere pattern.

Its functions are to alter the shape of an organ and withstand its internal load: it constricts tubes, changes volume and creates peristaltic waves. Single-unit sheets are electrically coupled by gap junctions and often spontaneously active. Multi-unit cells are more independently and densely innervated (e.g. iris, vas deferens, piloerectors).

Course content · section 2

Excitation, Ca²⁺ and cross-bridge cycling

Autonomic signaling, spontaneous potentials, hormonal stimuli, local factors or stretch may initiate activity. Voltage-dependent L-type calcium channels and receptor-mediated calcium signaling increase cytosolic Ca²⁺; calcium also comes from the SR.

↑ cytosolic Ca²⁺ → Ca²⁺–calmodulin → MLCK → myosin light-chain phosphorylation → actin–myosin cross-bridge cycling → force

MLCK uses ATP to phosphorylate myosin. Cross-bridge detachment also requires ATP. Myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP) removes phosphate while cytosolic Ca²⁺ falls to promote relaxation. By contrast, skeletal muscle uses Ca²⁺ binding to troponin for thin-filament regulation.

The lecture illustrates stimulus-driven action potentials, repetitive spikes triggered by slow waves and prolonged plateau potentials. It emphasizes voltage-gated calcium channels over fast sodium channels for smooth muscle action potentials.

Course content · section 3

Neural, chemical and hormonal regulation

Unlike the specialized skeletal neuromuscular junction, autonomic axons release transmitters from varicosities into diffuse junctions. Receptors determine excitatory versus inhibitory responses. The lecture contrasts epinephrine-mediated α₁ vascular constriction with β₂ bronchiolar relaxation.

Other inputs include NE, acetylcholine, epinephrine, cholecystokinin, angiotensin II, histamine, H⁺, O₂, CO₂, NO and membrane stretch. Smooth muscle often maintains basal tone, and its contraction reflects the balance among those signals.

Course content · section 4

Vascular smooth muscle and exercising muscle

Constriction: calcium entry or SR release increases, Gq signaling is activated, Ca²⁺–calmodulin promotes MLCK activity, and cyclic nucleotide/NO relaxation signaling decreases. Course receptors: α₁, AT₁ and V₁ (Gq); α₂ and 5-HT₁ (Gi).

Dilation: NO/cGMP or Gs/cAMP signaling increases, calcium entry falls with membrane hyperpolarization, and calcium removal into SR/out of the cell increases. The slides list A₂A and H₂ as Gs-mediated dilator receptors and note that phosphodiesterase inhibition preserves cAMP/cGMP.

Exercise raises sympathetic vasoconstrictor drive, but local low O₂, elevated CO₂ and H⁺ in active muscle favor vasodilation and blood flow. The tension-maintaining latch mechanism uses comparatively little ATP and helps smooth muscle sustain force across a wide range of lengths.

Course content · section 5

Skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle side by side

Key separation: smooth muscle lacks sarcomeres and T-tubules, uses calmodulin/MLCK to regulate myosin, has smaller SR stores and depends on both extracellular and SR Ca²⁺. Skeletal and cardiac muscle have sarcomeres and use troponin/actin regulatory control. Single-unit smooth muscle and cardiac muscle both have gap junctions, but skeletal muscle does not.

Check yourself: Why can the same catecholamine constrict one tissue and relax another? Why does an L-type Ca²⁺ channel blocker affect smooth muscle tone? Why is latch efficient?

Master these before moving on

  1. Dense bodies, no sarcomeres, no troponin.
  2. Single-unit gap junctions versus multi-unit discrete innervation.
  3. Ca²⁺–calmodulin → MLCK phosphorylates myosin; MLCP dephosphorylates myosin.
  4. α₁/Gq/Gi constrictor signals versus NO/cGMP and Gs/cAMP dilation.
  5. Local exercise metabolites can counteract sympathetic tone.

Selective First Aid connection: NO donors, PDE inhibitors and calcium-channel blockers affect these same vascular smooth-muscle pathways; these are board extensions, not additional lecture objectives.
